column6: The United States fast-tracked approval for the Thacker Pass mine and did not consult the Indigenous groups with claims to the land. There is opposition from 5+ tribal groups. This area contains the sites of two documented massacres that are critical moments in the history of these tribes. The Reno-Sparks Indian Colony (RSIC) and the Burns Paiute Tribe filed a lawsuit in July 2021 against the Federal Government and the Bureau of Land Management for failing to properly consult the tribes before permitting the mine. There are additional lawsuits filed by local ranchers and environmental organizations. As of 2026, all tribal federal permit appeals have been denied or settled with buyouts.
column9: "Our ancestors used this pass as a travel route, obsidian collection area, and campsite for thousands of years. Paiute and Shoshone people have hunted deer and other wildlife, fished for Lahontan cutthroat trout, gathered food and medicinal plants, and practiced our spiritual ways here since time immemorial, and we continue to do so to the present day. Sacred places like Peehee Mu'huh are our history and future. Our ancestors are buried in Thacker Pass and our young people visit this land to learn about the history of our people."

column6: The Atacama salt flat is home to roughly 25% of the world's lithium reserves, but the Atacama's Indigenous Lickanantay people have been protesting the lithium industry for decades. Large evaporation ponds for extracting lithium are depleting the already scarce water supplies. The reduction in water is also greatly impacting the local flamingo species, which see population decline as a result of the lithium mines. In 2025, the companies mining lithium and copper in the area made a commitment to working with the Indigenous groups and ensuring those communities benefit from the resource extraction as well. This caused a divide within the Indigenous groups as villages closest to the mines publicly disagreed with the arrangement. As of 2026, the mining companies came to a separate agreement with those villages.
column9: "Our deep connection to this place is based on what we have inherited from our ancestors: our culture, our language"

column2: Jujuy, Salta and Catamarca provinces, Argentina
column6: In the 2010s, Indigenous communities in the Puna region agreed to let two lithium mining companies operate in the area, hoping the mines would bring local jobs and economic development. Instead, the mines have jeopardized survival in one of the driest places in Argentina. Residents are so desperate for water that they are drinking from the Pastos Chicos River, which contains high levels of arsenic. In a single year, the lithium brining extraction utilizes more than 31 times the amount of water consumed by the local residents.
column9: "What are we going to do? Without [water] reserves, we’ll die"

column6: Jadarite is a rare, lithium-bearing mineral found nowhere else on Earth. The deposit in western Serbia is under eight farming villages with several thousand residents. The proposed mining project in this area stems from EU pressure to own more of the supply chain for lithium as a way to reach clean energy goals. Ever since the project was proposed in 2017, there have been continued protests by Jadar Valley residents over environmental and cultural concerns as the mining company began buying up residential areas. This proposal has turned into a large conflict between the EU, the Serbian government, the mining company, and Jadar Valley residents with multiple lawsuits filed. The Constitutional Court of Serbia ruled in favor of Rio Tinto, the mining company, in 2024, but after years of permitting issues, Rio Tinto halted the project in 2025.
column9: "There are things that money can’t buy. Our land, our roots, our home, our heritage are not for sale, nor are our souls... You do not have our permission to build a mine in the Jadar Valley! We will defend this country at the cost of our lives"

column6: Covas do Barroso is recognized by the UN as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System due to the ancestral knowledge and practices that are still maintained today. Savannah Resources is a London-based company building a large open-pit lithium mine in Covas do Barroso. Three-quarters of the lithium mine would be built on community-owned land. The Portuguese environmental agency approved the project in May 2023 as the EU aims to support more of the battery supply chain. Barroso’s agroecological system relies on the sustainable management of local resources.
column9: “I was 12 years old. My father got me a small hoe and told me to be careful not to fall into the water. I grew up connected to the land and was told I should take care of it... I chose to give continuity to what I inherited from my ancestors and to stay connected to the land.”
column21: "What makes this system so special is people’s strong connection to the land. Everything is done with a lot of care to sustainably manage the pastures, water and landscape.”
column23: ADRAT, the local development association that submitted Barroso’s application for world agricultural heritage

column2: Masvingo, Mashonaland East, Manicaland and Midlands provinces, Zimbabwe
column6: In 2025, Zimbabwe accounted for nearly 10% of the world’s lithium production; however, in 2026, the Zimbabwe government put a ban on all raw mineral ore and lithium concentrate exports in order to promote local value capture and beneficiation. Notably, Chinese companies dominate the lithium mining operations in Zimbabwe. The presence of these mines does not contribute to employment opportunities for locals, with most of the lithium sites having poor ratings by the local communities on their living conditions. At Buhera, 41 families were displaced. The displaced families asked for $3,000 but only received $1,000. Local graves were also exhumed, causing great emotional distress on local families.
column9: "Burying a child once is a burden no parent should bear, but to bury them again - to unearth the memories and relive the pain - is a heartache beyond measure."

column6: People in the remote town of Manono are desperate for lithium mines to get up and running, in hopes that these mines will transform the economic status of this rural area. The delays are due to ownership disputes between Australian and Chinese mining companies. So far, the Manono project has generated up to $28 million for mysterious shell companies, but has produced little for the DRC as it has not started to produce lithium or pay mining royalties.
column9: "There is wealth here. But, if you look closely, you will see that it’s the foreigners, people who don’t even dig themselves, who profit from our minerals and at our expense."
column21: " They exploit us — we are still colonized"
